title: Same Model. Different Precision. Different Footprint.

intro.before: Quantization stores weights in fewer bits so bigger models fit on smaller GPUs. The format decides
intro.after: , and which hardware can run it.

bullets.text: Stores weights in 8 bits: half of fp16
Keeps outlier features in fp16 for quality
Drop-in: load_in_8bit, no calibration
Often slower than fp16 at inference
Post-training 4-bit with calibration data
Pushes rounding error onto later weights
Widely supported fast GPU kernels
Needs a calibration set and quantize time
Finds salient weights from activation size
Scales them up before 4-bit rounding
No backprop; small calibration set
Mostly 4-bit, GPU-focused kernels
Single-file format for llama.cpp and Ollama
Runs on CPU, Apple silicon, GPU offload
Many levels, from Q8_0 down to Q2_K
Slower than GPU-native kernels at scale
16 levels spaced for normally shaped weights
Double quantization shrinks the scales too
The base format for QLoRA fine-tuning
Not the fastest format for serving
Floating point keeps dynamic range in 8 bits
Quantizes weights and activations
Native on NVIDIA Hopper and Ada GPUs
Needs recent hardware for the speed-up

principles.sub: 7B needs about 14 GB in 16-bit, 7 GB in 8-bit, 3.5 GB in 4-bit, plus KV cache.
GPTQ, AWQ or FP8 on GPU servers; GGUF on laptops, CPUs and Macs.
Compare quantized and full-precision outputs on your own eval set before shipping.

quote.big: Bits are a budget: spend them where it matters.
quote.small: Check quality on your task, not just size.
